title: Democrats Lead Polls Six Days Before Midterms as Trump, Obama Campaign
excerpt: A Reuters/Ipsos poll puts Democrats nine points ahead nationally and Kalshi traders give them a 63 percent chance of sweeping Congress, as Trump rallies in Texas and Ohio and Obama and Harris campaign in Georgia ahead of the November 3 vote.
body:
• A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted October 22-26 puts Democrats ahead of Republicans 47 percent to 36 percent nationally, widening to 50-41 when undecided voters' leanings are counted.
  • Prediction markets agree: Kalshi traders give Democrats a 63 percent chance of winning both chambers of Congress, and under 10 percent for a Republican sweep, CNBC reported.
  • President Trump's approval rating stands at 32 percent, and 73 percent of US adults say the cost of living is going in the wrong direction.
  • Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, with Republicans defending majorities in both the House and Senate and Senate races unexpectedly close in Texas, Kansas, Michigan and Ohio.

Six days before the US midterm elections, Democrats lead Republicans in national polling and prediction markets as both parties deploy their biggest names for the final stretch. President Donald Trump held two Republican rallies in Texas on Tuesday and heads to Ohio on Wednesday, while former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaign in Georgia for Democrats, Al Jazeera reported.

What the polls and markets say

A Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted October 22-26 found 47 percent of voters supporting Democrats against 36 percent for Republicans. When undecided voters' leanings were taken into account, Democrats led 50 percent to 41 percent. Trump's approval rating improved by one percentage point to 32 percent, and 73 percent of US adults said the cost of living was going in the wrong direction.

Prediction markets point the same way. Speculators on Kalshi place a 63 percent chance on Democrats winning control of both the House and Senate, odds that have stayed relatively stable since the beginning of October, CNBC reported via Political Wire. The chance of a Republican sweep is just under 10 percent, with a 29 percent chance that Democrats win the House while Republicans keep the Senate. Republicans are defending majorities in both chambers.

Senate races that were not supposed to be close

In Texas, where Democrats have not won a Senate election since 1988, Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are virtually tied. Trump has made four visits to the state in seven weeks — twice as many as at the comparable point before the 2024 election, Al Jazeera's Phil Lavelle reported from Corpus Christi — and local analysis suggests more Republicans than Democrats have voted early, though Talarico has been courting Republicans dissatisfied with Trump. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are in a closely contested Senate race.

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but Republican incumbent Roger Marshall faces a close contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton, a race that has drawn both Trump and Vice President JD Vance to the state. According to the Associated Press, both parties and their allied groups have committed about $71 million to advertising in the Kansas race, the most expensive Senate contest in the state's history. In Ohio, Republican Senator Jon Husted, who took over Vance's seat when he became vice president, faces former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat in 2024 and is seeking a return; more than $400 million had been spent or reserved for advertising in that race as of October 8, according to an Axios report cited by Al Jazeera.

The final days on the trail

At his Corpus Christi rally on Tuesday, Trump pointed to a tanker he said was carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan oil, suggested making Venezuela the 51st US state, and announced plans to roll back Biden-era restrictions on methane emissions from oil and gas production, saying it would help bring down energy prices. Secretary of State Marco Rubio joined Trump in Texas. In Alaska, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski has backed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor over the Trump-endorsed Bernadette Wilson.

On Wednesday, Trump speaks in Chillicothe, Ohio, his third rally in the state this month, and is scheduled to hold a rally in Iowa on Sunday. Vance will be in Kinston, North Carolina, campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper. In Georgia, Obama campaigns in Atlanta alongside Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, while Harris begins a three-day visit to the state, where early in-person voting ends on Friday, October 30.

For Indian-American voters, the stakes run through Congress itself: the party that controls the House and Senate after November 3 will control the committees and floor time for the immigration bills now moving through Washington, from H-1B thresholds to student work rules. Polls close on Tuesday, and control of both chambers will be decided by the handful of close Senate races both presidents are now flying into.
